title: US Monuments & Landmarks
description: Click on the map where you think this famous US landmark is located!

rounds.clue: France gifted this 305-foot copper lady to the United States in 1886. She holds a torch aloft in New York Harbor and a tablet inscribed with July 4, 1776.
Four presidents carved into a South Dakota granite mountain: Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt, and Lincoln. Sculptor Gutzon Borglum spent 14 years on it.
This 746-foot Art Deco suspension bridge painted 'International Orange' opened in 1937 and was once considered impossible to build.
Completed in 1884, this 555-foot obelisk in the nation's capital was the world's tallest structure for five years, built to honor the first president.
Lincoln sits in a massive marble chair gazing toward the Reflecting Pool. His Gettysburg Address and Second Inaugural Address are engraved on the interior walls.
This stainless steel arch in St. Louis soars 630 feet — as wide as it is tall — and serves as the 'Gateway to the West.'
Seattle's 605-foot tower was built for the 1962 World's Fair. Its rotating restaurant and flying saucer silhouette became a symbol of the Space Age.
Completed in 1931 during the Great Depression, this 102-story Art Deco skyscraper in Midtown Manhattan was the world's tallest building for 40 years.
This geyser erupts roughly every 91 minutes and has done so for centuries — it's the most famous feature of America's first national park.
These massive sandstone mittens on the Arizona-Utah border have appeared in countless Western films — John Ford shot many classic Westerns here.
This white marble memorial in Washington, D.C. overlooks the Tidal Basin and was built to honor the author of the Declaration of Independence.
A V-shaped black granite wall bears 58,000 names of Americans who died in Southeast Asia. Designed by a 21-year-old architecture student named Maya Lin.
This 630-foot-wide meteor struck 50,000 years ago and left a crater in Arizona that is nearly perfectly preserved — it's used by NASA for astronaut training.
Four miles of neon casinos, hotels, and entertainment venues in the Nevada desert that never turns the lights off.
Built during the Great Depression, this 726-foot dam on the Colorado River created the largest reservoir in the US and supplies power to several states.
The Hollywood sign on Mount Lee in Los Angeles originally read 'Hollywoodland' when it was erected in 1923 to advertise a real estate development.
This 1,451-foot skyscraper in Chicago was the world's tallest building from 1973 to 1998 — originally named after its developer, now called Willis Tower.
Fort McHenry in Baltimore survived a 25-hour British naval bombardment in 1814, inspiring Francis Scott Key to write what became the national anthem.
This cracked bell in Philadelphia bears the inscription 'Proclaim Liberty Throughout All the Land' — a quote from Leviticus — and rang at the first public reading of the Declaration.
Both the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution were debated and signed in this brick building in Philadelphia.
Three waterfalls straddle the US-Canada border here, creating the highest flow rate of any waterfall in North America — 750,000 gallons per second.
The 13-day siege at this 1836 Texas mission ended with every defender killed — including Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie. 'Remember' this place.
Every crewed American space mission since 1961 — from Mercury to SpaceX — has launched from this Florida facility.
Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay housed notorious criminals including Al Capone and Machine Gun Kelly — no prisoner ever officially escaped alive.
The Brooklyn Bridge took 14 years to build and opened in 1883 as the world's first steel-wire suspension bridge. Its chief engineer died before it opened.
The Wright Brothers made the world's first successful powered flight here on December 17, 1903 — covering just 120 feet in 12 seconds.
This 1,267-foot igneous rock formation in Wyoming was the first US National Monument (1906) — and featured in a famous 1977 Steven Spielberg film.
The USS Arizona Memorial in Pearl Harbor rests directly above the sunken battleship where 1,177 sailors were killed on December 7, 1941.
Over 50,000 soldiers became casualties at this Pennsylvania battlefield in July 1863 — the bloodiest battle of the Civil War, and site of Lincoln's famous address.
The Crazy Horse Memorial in South Dakota has been under construction since 1948 — when complete it will be the world's largest mountain carving.
Cadillac Ranch near Amarillo, Texas is an art installation where ten Cadillacs are buried nose-down in a wheat field — visitors spray-paint them daily since 1974.
Stone Mountain in Georgia features the world's largest bas-relief sculpture on a granite dome — you can hike to the summit or ride the cable car.
The Mackinac Bridge in Michigan connects the Upper and Lower Peninsulas across the Straits of Mackinac — one of the longest suspension bridges in the Western Hemisphere.
Muir Woods near San Francisco protects a cathedral grove of old-growth coastal redwoods — some over 1,000 years old — just 12 miles from the city.
The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel in Virginia is a 20-mile engineering marvel combining bridges, tunnels, and artificial islands spanning one of America's widest waterways.
Chimney Rock in Nebraska was the most-described landmark on the Oregon Trail — wagon train emigrants could see this spire for days before and after passing it.
rounds.answer: Chimney Rock National Historic Site, NE

rounds.clue: This 6,288-foot peak in New Hampshire holds the record for the highest wind speed ever recorded at an earthbound weather station: 231 mph in April 1934.
The world's largest natural bridge in southeastern Utah spans 275 feet across a canyon — longer than a football field — and is sacred to the Navajo people.
Where the Central Pacific and Union Pacific Railroads met in 1869, completing the first transcontinental railroad in US history.
rounds.answer: Golden Spike National Historic Site, UT

rounds.clue: Pueblo Bonito in northwestern New Mexico contains over 650 rooms and was the center of Ancestral Puebloan civilization around 850 to 1150 AD.
rounds.answer: Chaco Culture National Historical Park, NM

rounds.clue: This iconic Art Deco skyscraper on 42nd Street in New York City is crowned with an eagle gargoyle and a shimmering steel sunburst — briefly the world's tallest in 1930.
Portland Head Light in Maine is the oldest lighthouse in continuous operation in the US, commissioned by George Washington and lit in 1791.
The National Mall in Washington D.C. stretches nearly two miles from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial, flanked by 19 Smithsonian museums.
Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia River in Washington was the largest concrete structure in the world when completed in 1942.
A Cold War-era underground missile launch facility in South Dakota, kept on hair-trigger alert for 30 years and now open for public tours.
rounds.answer: Minuteman Missile National Historic Site, SD

rounds.clue: The Delicate Arch stands 52 feet tall in the Utah desert — completely freestanding with no support — and is the unofficial symbol of its state.
Cape Hatteras Lighthouse in North Carolina is the tallest brick lighthouse in the US at 198 feet, and was physically moved 2,900 feet inland in 1999 to escape erosion.
The World War II Memorial on the National Mall was the last major memorial added to the central axis in Washington, D.C. — dedicated in 2004.
Waikiki Beach in Hawaii is the birthplace of modern surfing in the United States — Duke Kahanamoku popularized the sport here in the early 1900s.
The Pony Express National Historic Trail stretches nearly 2,000 miles from St. Joseph, Missouri to Sacramento, California — this Missouri town is its starting point.
rounds.answer: Pony Express Start, St. Joseph, MO

rounds.clue: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech from the steps of this Washington, D.C. memorial overlooking the Reflecting Pool.
The Biltmore Estate in Asheville, North Carolina is the largest private home in the United States — 178,926 square feet with 250 rooms, built by George Vanderbilt.
Fallingwater in Pennsylvania is Frank Lloyd Wright's masterpiece — a house built directly over a waterfall, cantilevered over the stream.
This cable-stayed bridge in Charleston, South Carolina is the third-longest cable-stayed bridge in the Western Hemisphere, with a bike and pedestrian lane.
The Little Bighorn Battlefield in Montana marks where Lt. Col. George Custer and 268 soldiers were defeated by Lakota and Northern Cheyenne warriors in June 1876.
